1 1/2 oz Bounty Aged Rum (3/4 oz Hamilton's Demerara River 86° + 3/4 oz Coruba)
1 1/2 oz Pineapple Juice
1/2 oz Amaretto (Luxardo)
1/2 oz Coconut (Coco Lopez)
1/4 oz Lime Juice

Whip shake with crushed ice, pour into a Collins (double old fashioned) glass, and fill with crushed ice. Garnish with Angostura Bitters (3-4 dash), a cherry, and a "fucked up umbrella".
Two Fridays ago, I was looking for uses of my opened can of coconut cream, when I happened upon the Castaway at The Varnish in Los Angeles from their December 2018 menu through online recipe flashcards. The structure was very similar to their house Piña Colada with the addition of amaretto in place of some of the rum and the wind-swept inversion of their classic's paper umbrella. Amaretto has appeared in two tropical drinks on the blog, namely the 1937 Caribbean Punch and Kanaloa's more modern Ka Lima Lima Hema, so I was intrigued to try it here with the coconut. In the glass, the Castaway stranded the nose with clove aromas from the bitters garnish. Next, a creamy pineapple sip drifted over to rum, almond, coconut, and apricot flavors on the swallow.

We now know how the seeds of the NIST elliptic curves were generated: they’re not the hash of some saucy sentence, but the output of drand48 seeded with the time, which was indeed in 1997–98.

John Wood, Henry de Valence, Ava Howell, Zack Voase, Lucy Sweet, Amir Omidi, Paul Crowley, Iain McGinniss, Nicholas Carlini, and Steve Weis from Anthropic solved the riddle and on October 15th, 2026, at 01:07:51 UTC, claimed the full bounty I announced three years ago. They chose to donate the prize to ISRG, the non-profit that operates Let’s Encrypt, tripling its value to $36,864 (36 Ki$). Thank you to Amir Omidi, Chris Palmer, Colm MacCárthaigh, David Adrian, David Anderson, Jeff Hodges, Matt Green, Matthew McPherrin, Paul Kehrer, Ryan Sleevi, and Soatok for contributing to the bounty.

This helps fill out a page of cryptographic history, and reinforces our confidence in these critical cryptographic primitives.

The NIST elliptic curves (P-192, P-224, P-256, P-384, and P-521) were published by NIST in FIPS 186-2 in 2000. They were generated at random according to ANSI X9.62 by taking an arbitrary seed, hashing it with SHA-1, and using the output to derive some of the parameters. Until this week, we had no idea how those arbitrary seeds were picked.

The lore was that Dr. Jerry Solinas, who passed away in early 2023, generated them in 1997 by hashing some English sentences that he later forgot. You can read more in this article by Steve Weis or in the original bounty announcement.

Turns out memory can play tricks on everyone: we now know they were instead generated with the POSIX-standard drand48 random number generator.

The algorithm is as simple as passing the then-current UNIX timestamp to srand48() and then producing one byte at a time with drand48. Each sequence of 20 bytes is tried as a seed following ANSI X9.62 and rejected if the resulting curve is not valid. Some timestamps are used to generate multiple curves, by continuing to try seeds after accepting the first one. I reimplemented the algorithm in Go to verify the claim. Read more in Anthropic’s writeup.

There are two additional undocumented criteria beyond the ANSI X9.62 ones, one fairly clear and one that still escapes us.

If the bit length of the order n of the resulting curve is more than the bit length of the base field p of the curve, the seed is rejected. (The condition is not the stricter n < p, because prime239v2 has p < n < 2²³⁹.)

This leaves us with roughly twice as many valid seeds as were published. We explored a number of explanations for this last bit, and found no good fit. Maybe the same RNG was used to validate seeds, consuming RNG output and skipping some potential candidates, although the “gaps” are not regular. Maybe there was just a bug in one of the algorithms that returned the wrong result half the time; these calculations, which we can now do with off-the-shelf software in minutes, were still very much state-of-the-art in 1997.

  accepted 7026th seed bd71[...]: P-224

What does this mean for the security of elliptic curve cryptography based on the NIST curves? Well, even before this discovery there were no serious concerns among practitioners. In Section 3.1 of their 2015 paper “A riddle wrapped in an enigma,” Koblitz and Menezes make a convincing argument that it’s implausible that the NSA could have selected a seed to exploit a weakness that escaped more than 15 (now 25) years of cryptanalysis.

However, as reported in a later version of that paper, Daniel Bernstein and Tanja Lange described to Koblitz and Menezes in 2017 a technique that could have exploited 70 bits of freedom in selection of the seed to target a hypothetical class of 2⁶¹ weak prime-order curves. (Bernstein is the author of a competing elliptic curve design, Curve25519.) This contributed to enduring conspiracy theories, which had significant appeal among the non-specialist public (although many have since moved on to other, adjacent, conspiracy theories). All this speculation harmed confidence in robust cryptographic systems and was part of my motivation for the bounty.

This week’s findings completely rule out the technique described by Bernstein and Lange. Even if the NSA had been free to pick any timestamp in 1997–98 and any of the first 16 prime-order candidates (which generously accounts for the unexplained rejections), they would have had barely 30 bits of freedom. Not enough to intentionally target a hypothetical small class of weak curves, not enough to embed any kind of NOBUS backdoor.

Along with deterministic and hedged ECDSA signing algorithms, formally verified field implementations, and the 2015 complete addition formulas by Renes, Costello, and Batina, this nicely completes the “rehabilitation arc” of NIST elliptic curve cryptography, which I would now personally recommend over Curve25519/Ed25519/X25519.

Just in time for them to be retired in favor of post-quantum signatures.

P.S. The Anthropic team also figured out how the seeds of the NIST B-curves (the ones over binary fields) were generated, but no one uses those, so who cares.

The picture

In a FamilyMart in Taiwan I found this delightful dice set. A full roll carries log₂(6²⁰) ≈ 51.7 bits of entropy. Rolling them twice can make a pretty robust cryptographic key!

I thought it would be funny to label them as Geomys FIPS 140-3 Entropy Sources (which of course they are not, though we do have one of those) and hand them out as swag. However, I found no way to order them online, so I simply visited over a dozen FamilyMarts and brought home 50 packs.

Speaking of swag, I am 100% making stickers with the srand48() seeds, and t-shirts for the Anthropic team and the contributors to the bounty. I accept suggestions for other seed-based swag. If you want to catch some, follow me on Bluesky at @filippo.abyssdomain.expert or on Mastodon at @filippo@abyssdomain.expert.

people are failing a curiosity test right now. Armin Ronacher and Ben Vinegar had me on State of Agentic Coding to talk about it, along with DHH coming around, durable agents, a Lisp you program by talking to it, and why the labs cannot afford to fail.

Ben Vinegar (co-founder of Modem) and Armin Ronacher (Earendil, and the person most people know from Pi) run a podcast called State of Agentic Coding, and I was the guest for episode 11. Ben and I were in the same room in Toronto. I'd landed the day before after 22 hours of flying, I was there for two days, and then I was flying back to Sydney. Armin stayed in Vienna, sensibly.

We covered a lot of ground in an hour and a half. Here's the gist, written up properly, with chapter links at the bottom if you want to jump to a specific part of the conversation.

DHH did the funeral last week and he's right.

the curiosity test

Ben opened by asking what my contribution to the GDP of AI development has been from Ralph loops. The OpenRouter folks personally came up to me to say thanks for the uptick, so I know it has burned a lot of tokens. I published the research in July last year. When I first showed it to Cursor they thought it was garbage. Nine months later they'd implemented it, then Anthropic did it, then OpenAI did it, and now everyone's talking about loop engineering. Dex calculated it at about $10.42 an hour when you run it in the loop and it builds AFK overnight.

That weighed a lot on my shoulders when it first came out.

I've spent this year traveling the world giving talks, pleading with people to invest in themselves. My shortest take is this: software developers are failing a curiosity test. If you're displaced by AI as a software developer, it's self-inflicted, because you haven't been curious in a time of rapid transformation. As an employee, you trade time and skill for money. Employers' tastes are changing rapidly, but there's no reason you can't keep up with what's going on.

Just harshing everybody's vibe right out of the gate.

Ben pushed back here, and fairly. When people come into the industry they're young and have infinite time on their hands. Now many of them are in their thirties or forties and have racked up responsibilities. It's the same reason video games get harder to stay into as you age. It's hard to retool at this rate of change, and it's hard to feel optimistic when the thing at the centre of your income and your self-worth is in flux.

I concur. Dex Horthy has described my writing over the last two years as the depression era of Geoff: mourning the profession while pleading with people to be curious and to put themselves and their family unit first. This change has been forced on the world non-consensually. It displaces your identity. Are you a .NET developer? A Golang developer? A Python developer? It doesn't matter anymore. What matters is how good a developer you are, and whether you're using the thing employers now expect as the bare minimum.

Armin made a sharp observation: a lot of people in AI talk a very confident game externally, and that probably applies to us too. I'm straight up about this. I don't bloody know. Every time I discover something new, it strips me raw. You discover a new technique or capability, you thought you had a mental model of how it would play out, and then the game changes.

boom and bust

Ben, playing tour guide, pointed out that the closest US cities to Toronto are Buffalo and Detroit. Buffalo was once the third most populous city in the US, prosperous because of its rail access to the Great Lakes. It's now one of the most rapidly declining. Detroit is a later, similar story, tied to the auto industry. His point: there's a long history of people with hubris believing the good times will never end.

I've been through a few of these cycles, going back to the original dot-com boom and bust. Senior compensation went through the roof during the ZIRP era because, in the previous bust, we didn't develop enough talent. That created a scarcity of knowledge. Hold on, folks: the same cycle will repeat. CS enrolments are down; I remember seeing something like 22% in Singapore this year.

If you really love computers, you should be all in on loving computers right now. Everyone's having the time of their damn life. If you've stayed curious and kept your skills up to date, you can get placed anywhere right now. That means being able to stand at a whiteboard and explain how to build a coding agent as a sequence diagram, how inferencing works, and what a prompt cache is.

Armin had a slightly different read. Detroit not growing doesn't mean cars stopped being a thing; the industry went worldwide and commoditized. Software engineers got paid really well because we were scarce and our only competition was other software engineers. Automation didn't play a role. That's changing. He's absolutely convinced the exceptional role our profession has had over the last twenty years won't return in the same form. There will probably be a period with more demand for software engineers, but it will commoditize quickly. He's also curious what happens to San Francisco, a city that hasn't grown its housing stock, when the Anthropic IPO mints a pile of multi-millionaires competing for it.

I'm hoping for another PayPal-mafia-type thing. When people get minted, they invest in what they know.

dhh did the funeral

If you're in love with typing on a keyboard in an IDE, I'm sorry to say it, but DHH did the funeral last week, and he's right. You can still type code; you just do it in your personal workshop. Employers now want you to use the CNC machine and be very good with the CNC machine. They don't want artisanal woodworking anymore.

Ben summarised the Rails World keynote nicely. DHH walked through three generations of family pictures: a single drawing from his grandfather, a handful of photos from his childhood, and his kids with every second of their lives photographed. Portrait painting was an economic outcome. When photography made drawing reality uneconomic, painting went to impressionism and cubism: let's draw what isn't reality.

Armin had been on a panel at a Ruby conference in Austria earlier this year with Chad Fowler, who already said that the agent never writes Ruby for him anymore. When you sample which languages agents actually use, Ruby doesn't show up meaningfully. The online reaction to the keynote was largely dismissive, but the in-person reaction was much better received. Armin's point is that communities are disintegrating and reforming around the ideas that brought them together in the first place, even as the technology underneath changes. The Rails community is really a descendant of how DHH thinks software should be built; Ruby was just the tool.

So what's the point of a programming language or framework full of sugar designed for humans if humans aren't writing the code anymore? I've been chatting with the creator of Elixir, and he gets it. Language designers have dumbed down their languages to make them easy to learn for the human operator. All of that is falsified now that the agent writes the code. What does an agent need? What's the point of LSPs? Will we get new forms of interpretability, like an agent driving GDB, on a per-language basis? The languages won't go away, but the communities that swallow this tough pill and evolve will be the ones that survive.

Developers mostly speak to other developers. It's like a couple of cows in a field going moo to each other, completely missing that the cows are headed for the abattoir. Grim, I know. Stop being a cow. Learn a bit about business. Speak with founders and investors. Learn to be a product engineer. If you're working at a company that has banned AI outright, you should quit that company.

Armin said the strongest signal for him isn't his own belief; it's that the experienced, vocal holdouts are turning. DHH was dismissive early on. Notch was dismissive and recently turned. Ben noticed that DHH was transparent about having tried AI for design, pulled it back, and now landed firmly on the other side. It felt like an invitation: come join me. Armin's worry is that because DHH is polarising, the message may not land as widely as it should.

On where to find the signal: if you've been on X for the last two years, you're ahead of the game, because that's where all of this has happened. I don't love the platform; the number of AI reply bots is through the roof. But if you want the alpha, you have to push through. Go to the fediverse and talk about AI and you'll get your whole Mastodon instance banned. Bluesky has some high-alpha accounts. Unfortunately, the tech community has fractured along political lines, which means a lot of this isn't getting out.

Back in December 2024 I was writing that IDEs are dead as a product, and everyone called me crazy. I've taken a lot of unpaid time off work this year to give talks. You can't carry all that water yourself. The best you can do is this: if someone gets curious, help them get to their own moment. Find the thing that makes their mind explode, then ask them to show the next person. For me, that moment was seeing how easy it is to build a coding agent and realizing the entire game now is to build product recursively.

Ben brought up the Bob Dylan biopic with Chalamet. Dylan is folk royalty, goes electric, and the old caretakers practically call the police to shut it down while the younger audience wants the new stuff. Folk was one of the most popular genres of its time. The reason you know Dylan's name and not most of the folk scene's is that he evolved. Boy, we don't like change.

The one thing I wrote that really landed with juniors was "dear student, you're screwed". ThePrimeagen narrated it (thank you, Prime), and I wrote it as if I were giving career advice to my own kid at twenty. Now, at the AI Engineer World's Fair and in my travels, people come up and tell me they got a promotion because they turned up with the attitude and the skills. Don't thank me; you did the work. You were curious and you invested in yourself.

four months in 2026

Armin and the Earendil crew shipped Pi 1, and they also shipped something that's around 10,000 lines of code but took four months to build. Four months, in 2026. That's like a five-year project.

Armin's explanation is the bit I want everyone to hear. LLMs suck at the shape of a contract and the human feel of an API. You can express an idea really fast, but getting the right feel takes a lot of knowledge and experimentation. They solved the problem something like twenty times, each in about two hours, and none of those solutions felt right. The agent solves every problem in record time, but that doesn't give you a system with the right trade-offs. Finding the right trade-offs is what took four months.

The result is Pi Durable, which is how they now think an agent should be structured. You can shut down the harness, restart it, and it picks up exactly where it left off. That holds over the network, and through complex interactions such as sub-agents spawning and talking to each other.

Fourteen or fifteen months ago, Armin, Mario, Peter and others had a strong conviction that file systems and bash were the way to go, but nobody really knew how to build a harness around that. So everyone copied what Claude Code was doing, which is a very simple idea of a session: a transcript, a tool call, a tool result, in a loop. That model has stayed at the core of more or less every agent. At its simplest, all it does is automate copying and pasting.

But demands have changed. Background compaction means doing two things at once. A Slack experience means five people talking to the same agent, some in the same sub-thread and some branching off. That mapped incredibly poorly onto Pi's original design. Armin called it a little bit of cargo culting that we're all suffering from: we keep building on a basic primitive that causes pain everywhere. We don't notice, because an agent will happily build you a decent-looking agent, but under the hood it's messy, horrifying and not reliable.

this technology is moving really, really quickly and is held back by ideas about how it should work that are a year plus old.

Can I get that louder and printed on a shirt? Here's my hot take: your AGENTS.md and many of your skills should be deleted after every model release, or at least every couple of months, and redone. We carry so much that we think of as best practice, and we perpetuate it. Steering messages versus follow-ups were a UX paradigm; the loop underneath stayed the same. Async tasks for bash were one of the last big advancements. Go further back: why do we even have a shell? Because we used to have a human operator. If that need had never existed, would we have an operating system shell at all? That's the level at which we need to rethink the substrate.

a lisp you grow by talking to it

Ben asked what we'd actually thrown out lately, so I showed the thing I'd published that morning. We've raised two generations of software developers who have probably never seen Lisp and what it can do. Armin was very curious, because three months earlier he'd given a talk saying Lisp was the worst language for agents since they're terrible at counting closing parentheses. That's the old joke.

The usual mental model of a coding tool goes like this: you prompt it, it runs bash to look at your project, finds the file and uses the edit tool to change it. Then comes compilation, then CI/CD, then code review. What I showed throws all of that out.

I've connected an LLM to a running Lisp. I asked what functions were defined, and the LLM asked the running image. I asked for a string reverse function, typos and all, and it defined one directly into the image. Then string uppercase. Then a function to fetch a URL and parse the JSON. I can undo a change and roll back to the previous generation. There are only two tool calls in the inferencing loop: evaluate an expression, or define one as a function. I'm editing the Lisp image and its runtime environment through a chat. Once a function is defined, it's defined.

Now don't think of this as a chat interface. Imagine you're logged into your website and there's a secret little Hackers-style menu that only shows for staff. You don't load up an IDE. You pop a prompt and evolve the running program by chatting with it. What if that's how a user feedback request gets actioned?

Ben mentioned that the opencode folks had just written about how much work it took to make individual plugins hot reload, never mind be programmed live. Armin said that on a single-player level this is very much what made Pi interesting, since Pi can rebuild and reload itself. The challenge is that JavaScript is not a language built for hot reloading.

why lisp died

Ben's question was the right one: if this is so fantastic, why does it feel like you're digging up a grave?

Lisp has always been about these things. But you had to be a Lisp programmer to do Lisp. Now there's a natural-language interface that lets anyone do Lisp-type stuff. Armin gave the more precise answer. The problem with software is effects. That's partly why Pi Durable exists: if you shut down Pi and reload it, it doesn't come back exactly as it was, because not everything is serialisable. Lisp can serialise its entire state out more than most languages can, and functions are defined much like data.

Why did it go away? Lisp was slow unless you had a machine that really suited it, and it didn't survive the shift to the personal computer, where people wrote assembly. Armin's bluntest point: it's a horrible language to look at. It's awful for humans. Maybe it's great for LLMs. Many of our trade-offs as engineers exist because we're lazy and pick the things that let us stay lazy.

That's the Ruby thing again: designed to be beautiful and easy for humans, but less powerful. Paul Graham's Beating the Averages covers this with the Blub paradox.

I also want to give credit to Krzysztof Cieślak. He doesn't get credit for it, but he's the person behind what everyone now calls spec-driven development. He's at GitHub Next, he's one of the people behind Ionide for F#, and he published research back in the GPT -3 era asking whether Markdown could be the future of how we publish software. When I was doing my Ralph loops, I remembered his research and thought: the models got better, let's redo it. The rest is history. For the record, though: code is the spec, folks. Markdown is not a spec. As Armin put it, there are specifications and there are vibe specifications.

Someone took the Lisp idea and vibed up a web app version in about an hour. It's not Lisp; Lisp is just an easy way to express the idea, nerd snipe people and teach a new generation that powerful languages exist even when their developer experience is terrible. Who cares about the developer experience now that agents write the code? He clicks a little developer button, prompts the functionality in, and the app saves a generation. Think about what that means for someone in sales, marketing, finance or legal: building the product by chatting with the product. This is a completely different way of designing a coding harness. The programming language is LLM-enabled, rather than a harness producing code for a programming language. If you want to be a nerd, go and do this with Smalltalk. You'll be on the front page of Hacker News tomorrow, guaranteed.

Ben compared it to interviews with musicians like Beck, who pull records off the shelf in their office, or hip-hop producers digging through forgotten lore. I'm pulling out my old Smalltalk and Lisp records. He called me old. It's worth going back to the classics and doing some sampling.

code mode and code golf

Armin has noticed the models changing. Harnesses are increasingly having the model write code to make tool calls. I've seen the same thing: the models aren't going for the edit tool anymore. They're doing a kind of program synthesis, writing one-liner Python to edit files.

Armin said Pi supplies an edit tool, and in something like 80% of cases with the latest models it's no longer used. His theory has two parts. First, there's very little punishment in training runs for anything other than succeeding, so the models use whatever means they have. Second, that code behaviour is being trained into the models. Pi offers code mode as a tool and will probably make it the default: run some JavaScript instead of bash. Bash runs where your files are; code mode runs in the harness loop, which is typically the same computer but not necessarily.

The side effect is fascinating and a bit grim. Remember code golf, where you win by writing the shortest possible solution? That's what some of these models feel like. Single-character variables, no indentation, unreadable. Ben's read was that there's a real tension here: the tightest possible code is optimal for a tool-calling loop, but it isn't what you want in your application code. Armin's read was that it might not get punished much anymore, because the models are mostly rewarded for completion on synthetic benchmarks, and they're releasing faster than ever.

The last time it was like this was the Sonnet 3.5/3.7 era, which spewed Markdown everywhere and wrote those one-liners even though it had an edit tool. Then it went away. Now it's back. I was recently given access to a couple of racks of GB300s and have been running Kimi on them. You can feel the models diverging: Kimi reaches for the edit-file tool, while the frontier American models program their way around it over bash.

black-box agents

For our profession, we've been post-AGI for over a year now. By that I mean the models have been good enough to cause displacement for over a year. I'd rather focus on how beautiful it is that you don't need frontier intelligence for every task.

As much as you might want local models, they aren't really a thing yet unless you have a couple of million dollars of data centre hardware. That won't always be the case. I love open-weight models. Kimi is not as good output-wise, it's chattier and slower in its chain of thought, but I get to see the thinking traces. I'm permanently upset that the American frontier labs keep locking more of my stuff away.

Ben has noticed the desktop apps showing less and less of what's happening. You ask for a big piece of software and get three lines of output. Is that product design or technology?

Armin split it in two. Hiding thinking traces is the labs hating distillation, and we should call that out for the nonsense it is. Less tool output is the same reason Pi will probably soon hide tool output: when the model invoked harness-provided tools, you could build a UX around it ("now you're reading a file"). Now that it's running unreadable code, you'd need a second LLM just to explain what it's doing.

He thinks that's a regression for the user, the model and the lab. Approvals are mostly gone. But if you're using an agent for something truly critical, like medical research or fully verified programs, you can't just take its word at the end.

You want verification along the way. One possible future is two streams: the code being generated, and a commentary stream from another model explaining what's going on. We already run smaller models alongside larger ones for speculative decoding. But do you really want to pay extra tokens to find out what's happening?

I backed him on that. When we built Amp, a lot of it was UX design: animations and components keyed to the type of tool, whether it was an edit or a git patch. When everything is just bash, there's no way to know what it's doing without running a classifier over the tool calls. That's what the big harnesses are doing now: classifiers and parallel things in the background, chewing more tokens.

Here's a brainworm. How much of agentic design is constrained by not busting the prompt cache, because everyone is financially sensitive to it? If you removed that restriction, what would you build? I think it would allow some really cool stuff.

Armin is excited about fast classifier models for LLM-sized problems at much higher speeds; every morning he uses one to sort open issues and compare them to yesterday. But he called the KV cache an innovation killer. It locks you into an ecosystem, at least for the duration of a session, so you can't switch models mid-session. It's got worse: on some frontier models, a cache miss from a prefix change now loses all your reasoning. That's driven by distillation fear, and it's one more reason open-weight models have a good future. They allow experimentation.

I'm very long on open-weight models. They've been good enough for the last year and lag the frontier by about three months; the hardware is what's missing. American open-weight efforts like Reflection are starting to show up too.

tech demo land

Look at the frontier labs' go-to-market motion. It's an AWS play: commit now to reserved capacity and pre-commit, and you get a discount. They're asking people to lock into an ecosystem before a winner has been declared. Two weeks ago OpenAI was king; now we're back to loving Claude.

Ben had a conspiracy-brain theory. All the models write decent code now, so that's no longer the differentiator. Are capabilities trained in deliberately and then seeded through influencers? When one model came out, everyone was suddenly making games and 3D models. When Opus 5.5 came out, videos of it making EDM-pop music videos appeared out of nowhere.

Armin doesn't think every release will be punctuated like that, and his reason is the important one. Forcing himself to pay API prices changes how you look at all of it.

I am burning more virtual money than I'm earning.

That's ridiculous. This is tech-demo land more than sustainable-business land, and eventually someone will want a return. His favourite example: a $20 CarPlay adapter from China with a system on a chip. You can hack it, so now it runs his little agent and his car dashboard shows a crappy version of Pi. It was $20 for the hardware and $15,000 in tokens. He would never have paid $15,000 for a side project. At $200 he still wouldn't have bothered. He does it because he rotates subscriptions.

Ben has been doing the same with Blender scenes, a Toy-Story-esque ad and 3D-printed replacement parts. Any rational pricing would say just order the part on Amazon.

Two things can be true. Either a random account making a magical discovery was genuinely curious, and curiosity is the limiting factor in society right now. Or that person is part of a campaign, like a game developer planting an Easter egg nobody finds and then going to a games magazine to do an exposé. It's happened before in our industry. (Ben has a bunch of Modem Easter eggs on his website that nobody has found. ATDT.)

People call me the token guzzler, the subscription killer. A year ago I went viral on Reddit as one of the top users; I'm the clown that blew through the quotas. If you're using OpenAI models, there's a thing called underclass on my GitHub that lets you pool multiple subscriptions.

It still makes sense to have ten of them, because they're so heavily subsidised. But you don't need frontier intelligence for everything. Maybe just get a GLM coding plan, which used to be about 300 bucks for the entire year.

They're subsidised for a reason. The labs want to build addictive behaviour at home, so that when you go to work you think: if I can build my wildest dreams at home, why can't that magic happen here? No one can pay the real cost of these tokens. I'd be up past US$200,000 a month at real prices. I hit these slot machines hard for about ten days, watching the inferencing and the behaviours. Then I throw my computer away and don't look at it for a week or two, because you've done six months of work in a week and you need to self-care. I've seen what happens when you don't. One of the first people I showed the Ralph loop to fully cooked himself: he teleported into the future, built everything he'd planned for retirement, didn't sleep, and was unable to work for nine months.

On a lighter note, my twelve-year-old has been playing Magic the Gathering and making friends, which is great. He's also been 3D printing custom card boxes. I'm putting this on tape so I can show him when he's eighteen: I've noticed that every box, every week, is hyper-personalised with the name of a different girl in his class.

Ben suggested I send him the bill at the real token price.

Ben's sharper point: if a general model can write music, generate those videos and drive Blender, do you still need the vertical model companies? Maybe you just need a Claude subscription.

the labs cannot fail

Put your financial accounting hat on. The labs have raised so, so much money, and we're entering a higher-interest-rate environment. The bond market is changing. If you borrow money, you need an ROI above the bond rate. They very much cannot fail, which means everything is on the table to be absorbed into your Claude subscription. I could see Runway inside Claude, maybe even through an acquisition. At this level of capitalisation, nothing is off the table.

Armin was more measured: some people win, some lose. He thinks it will most likely work out, but there are no guarantees. I think the financials are cooked. The ROI over the new bond rate needs an adoption curve far steeper than the human adoption curve, and that gap is going to be very hard for the labs.

Both things can be true at once. I haven't written code by hand in about two years, and I'm never going back. This is transformational. If it all blows up, I'll run GLM or Kimi on some data centre hardware myself and be fine. My profession has been transformed, and I'm not going back to how it was, but I'm in no way hyper-dependent on any one lab.

who wants this?

Ben brought it back to my demo, and fairly. He doesn't know that many people actually want to change their website or app by talking to it. Technologists look at all the incredible stuff we can do through the lens of software malleability, but that's not society at large. Most people want to use software, not change it every session. He's been running Omarchy for about a year and only now let himself customise it, for about an hour, to make it nicer for his family. That's probably the interaction.

I'll play with that. Society at large does not want an assistant, folks. Only type-A people who already have an executive assistant want one. When I get automated emails that are obviously AI, I block them. I'm actually seeking out humanity as everyone else rushes to automation. Search Instagram and TikTok for AI data centres and you'll find people who want to burn them down. In business, though, people do want to change their software without having to talk to someone and switch between tools.

Armin's ending thought: while we were recording, someone proposed two potential new superconducting materials that Opus 5.5 found. It gave him LK-99 flashbacks. He doesn't think it matters that we're all obsessed with AI for software engineering. Where this really pays out is if we get room-temperature superconductors, or whatever else we might find.

if it's just going to be a bunch of programmers who are now producing slop, I'm pretty sure society will just burn the data centers down.

We'll know the labs are ready to IPO when they've found a cure for cancer. That's what changes society's heart. That's always been the narrative.

Then again, the average person doesn't really care. TikTok has been very anti-AI lately: people see something is AI and won't like or reshare it. But there's an AI-made song doing the rounds about an Irish girl that I can't describe on a family-friendly podcast. Young women are showing it to their mothers to film the shocked reaction, and for the first time people are saying, "I don't care if this is AI, it slaps."

We call things slop because we're playing with a new creative medium and don't yet know what isn't slop. We're all just trying to figure out what's changing.

Yesterday's slop is today's content.

I have to say, Peter Steinberg (aka lobster man) is absolutely brilliant. He was so ahead of his time with OpenClaw. I remember when he first tweeted about it last year, and when it turned into utter lobster madness at the beginning of the year.

Heck, I even ran OpenClaw for a bit, but I couldn't really see the value because I didn't want to maintain it while the lethal trifecta problem remains unsolved.

Categorically, this is a billion-dollar problem, perhaps more.

So here's the thing. I kind of want openclaw, but I want it managed. For almost a year now, I've been using Interaction Labs Poke, because if there's going to be a problem with the lethal trifecta, I want to make that problem someone else's as much as possible. I want them losing sleep over the lethal trifecta, not me. It's not full protection, but knowing there's a product team paid to think about these issues and resolve them at scale puts me at ease.

That is, until last week, when Poteto girl nerd-sniped me on X and, in full disclosure, hooked me up with enough credits to help me reevaluate. I am now using Grokbot full-time instead of Poke (which sucks), and I've revisited my priors about the utility of an AI bot and who they are useful for.

I'm writing this blog post of my own free will in the hope that it will help change some other people's perspectives on the utility of these assistants and give people some ideas on how they can be used, but most importantly, to highlight the risks of using these types of tools.

In this post, I'm going to give a high-level overview of how I've automated some aspects of my life. Late to the game, I know, but with some things it's better to be cautious.

initial experiences

Okay, Grokbot is really weird, and I guess this applies to, like, even OpenAI's dots, even though I have not used it. One of the hardest things about it is how generic it is. Once you have it installed, it becomes a question of "now what?"

You need to be curious, have lots of imagination, and when you have an idea, just ask for it. From that point forward, it starts to unfold like a pretty flower. If functionality is missing, ask for it and turn it into a skill.

starter pack

If you're using Grok, install this skill pack first, and use it to create other bots. Every time you need a new bot, which is often, ask this bot to create one.

some ideas for bots

Here are the bots I've defined in the last week, which I'm getting a lot of utility out of:

Daily briefs and reporting

  • Daily Update sends the 7am brief: calendar, emails that need a reply, and site traffic. Connectors: Google Calendar, Gmail, PostHog.
  • Blog Pulse reports on the health of https://ghuntley.com/newsletter: signups, unsubscribes, churn, MRR, and traffic. Connectors: Ghost Admin API (direct read-only, no connector), Stripe (read-only), PostHog (read-only).
  • Inbox Diet finds newsletters worth unsubscribing from and lists them for you to click yourself. This is by far one of my favorite bots. I have unsubscribed from so many newsletters via this bot, probably upwards of 300, that would be too hard to do by hand. Finally, my inbox is under control. Connector: Gmail.
  • Family sends a digest of WhatsApp messages related to my kids, does reminders, and automatically extracts classwork and homework reminders from school emails. Connectors: Gmail, bidirectional access to my WhatsApp via the WhatsApp bot. A custom parser for Seesaw that can retrieve updates sent by my kiddos' teachers.
  • WhatsApp answers lookups of my WhatsApp messages acts as a function pipe for bots. Connector: WhatsApp Web in a browser, with no connector behind it. The bot can tunnel to my Mac Mini, read the WhatsApp message database directly, and send messages, but it can't send messages from the Mac Mini. To do that, you need to authenticate in a browser session, which allows two-way communication.

Money, tax and legal

  • PocketSmith keeps my spending categorized and my budget up to date. PocketSmith already has pretty good categorization rules built in, but they normally rely on the user to train PocketSmith. Here, I use an LLM to do the categorization automatically. It is good. Connector: none; it calls the PocketSmith REST API directly.
  • Australian Tax continually prepares a rough first draft of my personal tax records for each financial year. Connectors: Gmail, plus the PocketSmith bot.
  • Bank Details shares my bank details with your other bots when they need them. Connector: none; the details are stored as a secret.
  • Conference Reimbursement is one of my favorite bots. Conferences normally work on the basis that they will pick up your flights once you've done the talk, which always carries this risk that you won't be reimbursed. If it's a professional conference, then you get paid up front, but sometimes the community conferences have cash flow problems because they haven't sold all their tickets yet. So normally it's a gentleman's handshake that they'll reimburse, but sometimes these conferences don't reimburse me. For example, right now I'm probably out close to $10,000 in travel expenses this year. When these situations arise, I ask Dr. Egg Bot to create a reimbursement reminder bot. That bot has access to my email, WhatsApp, and everything else, and it can automatically query PocketSmith to see whether the reimbursement has landed. If it hasn't landed, it will ask me for permission to send a WhatsApp message or an email to nudge people along. Connectors: Gmail, WhatsApp bot.

Life admin

  • Kitten Vet tracks the kittens' vaccinations and vet admin and automatically reminds me of what I need to do for them. Connectors: Gmail, Google Calendar.
  • Desires keeps my bucket list and "someday" list. Connector: Google Calendar and X. What's really cool is that sometimes I'll have a conversation out in public and genuinely want to catch up with someone, but I forget. So I can just prompt my desires bot to like add it to the particular category, either by searching X or dropping the exact link of the conversation.

Dev and infrastructure

  • Mac Mini operates the Mac mini. It's a function pipe bot. Tailscale is installed on the Linux machine the bot runs on; it's on my Tailscale network and can tunnel its network connectivity out via my Mac Mini as needed to bypass any geo-blocks on data center IP addresses.
  • Overalls manages my upcoming open-source project called Overalls (previously known as loom) and acts as a remote interface for dispatching agentic coding tasks in ephemeral Firecracker VMs hosted on my self-hosted infrastructure.

lessons learned

What you want to do is to create bots thinly. You don't want a fat bot. You want to create a bot per function. Think about the Unix command line, how composable that is. You want to create small bots that can call other small bots, then pipe them together in a function chain.

You can install software on your Grok bot. For example, I have Tailscale installed, and that's how I do all my tunneling.

the future

If the lethal trifecta is ever solved at a fundamental level, I'll move all this stuff into a self-hosted Open Claw, but not before. I get the value of OpenClaw, and they do a good job with security, but fundamentally, I sleep much better at night knowing there's a product team whose arse is on the line, with staff and a funded security organization with a security VDP program that loses sleep over these topics, so I don't have to.

The Go Blog

Interactive refactoring in gopls

Hongxiang Jiang
16 October 2026

When editing code in a modern IDE or editor, developers rely on its refactoring features to automate common transformations. Today, we are excited to introduce interactive refactoring in gopls, powered by a new capability we are proposing for the Language Server Protocol (LSP) that brings dynamic, multi-step dialogs directly into your favorite editor. Crucially, we designed this capability (in collaboration with the Dart team) not just for Go, but as an open standard for all programming languages and editor ecosystems. Working support is already available in gopls v0.24.0 and the official Go extension for VS Code v0.56.0.

What is the Language Server Protocol (LSP)?

The LSP is an open standard that decouples language-specific features from specific text editors. As you navigate and edit code, your editor (such as VS Code, Neovim, or Emacs) and a language server (like gopls) engage in a continuous JSON-RPC exchange to provide features like autocomplete, hover documentation, diagnostics, and code actions.

Multi-step code transformation

Today, almost every code transformation in the LSP is like a function of no parameters: you trigger the operation, and the server immediately computes the edits. (Renaming a symbol is the sole exception: because it is a function of one parameter, the desired new name, it required its own dedicated PrepareRename RPC in the protocol.)

"Add struct tags", without questions

The language server must deduce the user’s intent from context alone, namely the cursor position and the enclosing syntax tree. When that context is not enough, the server is forced into one of two choices: apply a one-size-fits-all default, or refrain from offering the transformation altogether. The limitation lies not in gopls’s ability to compute the necessary edits, but in the LSP’s lack of a mechanism for language servers to ask the user for input.

For many transformations, this parameterless model works well. But many others need additional input from the user: which struct tags to add and in what naming convention, which interface to implement, which file to move a declaration to. Without a way to ask, gopls could only guess—“Add struct tags”, for example, always produced json tags in camelCase—or not offer the refactoring at all. With interactive refactoring, language servers can now easily provide new operations with one or more parameters.

"Add struct tags", with questions

While some language extensions have worked around this limitation by embedding custom, language-specific dialog logic directly into individual editors, doing so leaves behind other editors (such as Neovim and Emacs) that stick strictly to the LSP with minimal custom client code. More importantly, editor-specific workarounds go against the fundamental purpose of the LSP: to decouple language-specific features from editors so that each server improvement benefits every client.

Our LSP interactive refactoring proposal (microsoft/language-server-protocol#1164) solves this by establishing a standard mechanism for language servers to collect user input before computing text edits. For Go developers, this unlocks a suite of long-awaited refactorings, including:

  • golang/go#70583: Move Declaration
  • golang/go#38028: Change Signature
  • golang/vscode-go#1547: Implement Interface
  • golang/vscode-go#2002: Modify Struct Tags

among many others.

Interactive refactorings in action

Adding and removing struct tags (gopls v0.23.0)

When configuring serialization formats, developers frequently need custom tags and casing conventions. Previously, running “Add struct tags” unconditionally injected json tags using camelCase formatting.

With interactive refactoring:

  1. Place your cursor on any struct definition and select the “Add struct tags” code action.
  2. An input dialog appears, pre-filled with json, allowing you to customize any combination of tags (such as json,yaml,db).
  3. A second dialog lets you select your desired naming convention (such as camelCase, snake_case, or PascalCase).
  4. Gopls generates and applies the formatted struct tags across your type definition.

Interactive "Add struct tags" in VS Code

Here is the before-and-after transformation:

type UserProfile struct {
    ID        int64
    FirstName string
    LastName  string
    EmailAddr string
}

type UserProfile struct {
    ID        int64  `json:"id" db:"id"`
    FirstName string `json:"first_name" db:"first_name"`
    LastName  string `json:"last_name" db:"last_name"`
    EmailAddr string `json:"email_addr" db:"email_addr"`
}

Similarly, “Remove struct tags” now asks you for the specific tag keys you wish to delete (for example, removing only db tags while preserving the json tag), rather than wiping out all struct tags indiscriminately.

Interactive "Remove struct tags" in VS Code

Implementing interfaces with dynamic symbol search

When creating a type to satisfy an interface, developers previously had to copy the interface declaration and manually turn it into a set of methods on the receiver type (or rely on external tools like impl by manually typing the receiver and qualifying the name of the interface).

Since gopls v0.23.0, with interactive refactoring:

  1. Place your cursor on any concrete type and select the “Add methods to X to implement an interface…” code action.
  2. A text entry field appears, inviting you to choose the name of an interface type. It makes dynamic queries to gopls to auto-complete names of types in your workspace and the standard library (for example, maphash.Hasher).
  3. If the selected interface has type parameters, gopls asks for a concrete type argument for each type parameter (such as Foo).
  4. Gopls generates complete method stubs with appropriate receiver names and instantiated method signatures.

Interactive "Add methods to implement an interface..." in VS Code

type Foo struct{}

type MyHasher struct{}

type Foo struct{}

type MyHasher struct{}

// Equal implements [maphash.Hasher].
func (m *MyHasher) Equal(x Foo, y Foo) bool {
    panic("unimplemented")
}

// Hash implements [maphash.Hasher].
func (m *MyHasher) Hash(*maphash.Hash, Foo) {
    panic("unimplemented")
}

Moving declarations across files and packages (preview)

Moving declarations manually by cutting and pasting can easily break references and requires tedious import cleanup across multiple files. While scheduled for an upcoming gopls release, our working implementation already demonstrates how interactive file selection streamlines cross-file and cross-package moves:

  1. Place your cursor on any top-level declaration and select the “Move declaration X” code action.
  2. A file picker dialog lets you choose an existing destination .go file or specify a new file path.
  3. Gopls moves the declaration along with its dependent declarations (such as unexported helpers or methods) while leaving unrelated symbols in place, updates references across your workspace, and cleans up imports in both the source and destination files.

Interactive "Move declaration" in VS Code

In the example below, we move the type Foo from package from to package to. Its method Print and the unexported constant bar, which only Foo uses, move along with it, while the unrelated function Baz stays behind:

// from/from.go
package from

import (
    "fmt"
    "strings"
)

const bar = "bar"

// Doc comment for Foo
type Foo struct{}

func (f Foo) Print() {
    fmt.Println(bar)
}

func Baz() string {
    return strings.ToUpper("baz")
}

// from/from.go
package from

import "strings"

func Baz() string {
    return strings.ToUpper("baz")
}

// to/to.go
package to

import "fmt"

const bar = "bar"

// Doc comment for Foo
type Foo struct{}

func (f Foo) Print() {
    fmt.Println(bar)
}

Slaying the dragon (gopls v0.24.0)

As a demonstration of multi-step interactive dialogs and a self-contained test case for client editor implementations, gopls v0.24.0 offers a “Slay the dragon” code action when you place your cursor on a package-level variable named dragonSlayer (for example, var dragonSlayer string). Happy hunting!

What’s on the Horizon

Interactive refactoring establishes a foundational capability in gopls, opening up several exciting directions on our roadmap:

  • Change signature refactoring (#38028): Adding, removing, or reordering function parameters across a workspace requires input that cannot be deduced from syntax alone, such as the new parameter order or the default argument expression to insert at existing call sites. Interactive forms allow gopls to collect these details before rewriting the declaration and all call sites.
  • Interactive conflict resolution: When a code transformation encounters naming collisions, identifier shadowing, or ambiguous references, gopls can ask the user for guidance, such as asking for permission to proceed or offering to rename conflicting symbols on the fly.
  • Interactive commands beyond code edits: Because interactivity is modeled at the LSP command layer, it naturally generalizes to non-edit server operations that require user configuration, such as configuring test or benchmark runs with profiling flags (CPU, memory, tracing).

Getting Started and Sharing Feedback

Interactive refactoring is available in gopls v0.24.0 and vscode-go v0.56.0 (with proof-of-concept client integrations also explored for Neovim and Emacs).

We would love to hear your thoughts as we continue refining interactive code actions in gopls:

  • For general feedback or feature requests, file an issue on the Go issue tracker.
  • To read the full technical specification—including the stateless form protocol design and alternative approaches we explored—or to join the discussion with the broader LSP community, check out the LSP Interactive Code Actions design document and the ongoing conversation in microsoft/language-server-protocol#1164.

(Special thanks to Alan Donovan, Alex Putman, Brian Wilkerson, Danny Tuppeny, Hana Kim, Madeline Kalil, Peter Weinberger, and Robert Findley for their insights, discussions, feedback, and collaboration on this work.)

Happy refactoring!

If AI is so great, why aren’t we seeing an explosion of new, amazing software products? If anyone can turn their idea into working software with coding agents, where is all that software? People have been asking this question for years. As far as I can tell, the answer is that it’s spread out over a lot of modestly successful projects:

  • Somewhere between 2x and 20x new software is being created, depending on where you look
  • There’s no real growth in massively successful software projects (not counting AI tools)
  • There is around 2x growth in modestly successful software projects

Where all the new software is

I picked1 around twenty separate sources — software marketplaces, plugin registries, modding platforms, etc — which expose installation counts. I then compared the number2 of successful software projects between 2022-24 and 2025-26: i.e. before and after agentic coding hit the mainstream in mid-2025.

There’s a clear jump in modestly (not wildly) successful projects. For instance, the NVDA screen-reader addons directory had a bit over twice as many new addons with more than a thousand downloads (though no change in addons with more than ten thousand). The HACS open-source home automation community plugins store likewise saw twice as many new addons with over a hundred installs but no change in ones with over a thousand. New Steam games with over a hundred reviews are about 60% more common now than pre-2024. Obsidian plugins, Firefox and Chrome extensions, Nexus game mods, and Blender extensions had the same pattern. The Google Play store, WordPress plugins, and a few others didn’t show this pattern, but I think it’s still enough to conclude that AI is indeed driving a boom in hobbyist software.

Why addons and plugins?

I think examining addons, mods, and plugins is useful for a few reasons. First, it’s usually pretty easy to tell how many people are using them, or at least have installed them. Obviously AI is letting people produce a lot of software — I work at GitHub, so I see this first-hand — but without checking installation counts it’s unclear how much of this is actually being used.

Second, it’s a good way to minimize the amount of software that’s about AI. It doesn’t tell us much about AI’s effect on software to point out all the successful software projects that help people code with AI. That’s just selling shovels. The real question is whether AI is helping generate software that solves people’s ordinary problems.

AI-generated game mods and ports are a great example of this, because gamers aren’t trying to change the world with AI coding. They just want to play multiplayer Halo CE in the browser, or fly a plane in Helldivers, or play Super Smash online with rollback netcode. It’s looking like3 AI can supply this need effectively.

Were these projects actually AI generated?

Everyone is very coy about AI usage in hobbyist communities. In the rare cases where people admit it, they often get dogpiled. People really don’t like AI, even when it’s producing software they find useful. Given that, I don’t think it’s possible to use voluntary AI disclosure data to figure out whether AI is driving a software boom: the presence of the tag itself will discourage use, and many developers are just not going to admit it.

A 2x growth in successful projects between 2022-24 and 2025-26 is clearly something to do with AI, particularly in the background of a 10x growth in total projects. Of course not all of these projects will have AI involvement. But when people ask “why hasn’t AI improved software”, they’re talking about a missing trend4: wondering where all the new software is. As it turns out, it’s going towards a lot of small software projects that a few hundred or thousand people find useful.

Why small, moderately successful projects?

Why is AI growth visible in small projects but not big software companies? Why is it concentrated in moderately successful products and not wildly successful ones? I don’t have any data for this, but here’s my speculation.

Big, successful software companies often have all the visible features they want. That’s why there’s not a wild explosion of new features in, say, macOS or Gmail: what would those features even be? As I’ve written about before, they’re also technically paralyzed by the features they have, so it’s not trivial for even very good coding agents to add new ones. Finally, many new features in successful products are subtle (e.g. enterprise compatibility things that almost all users will never encounter, or purely internal systems that slightly increase reliability).

It’s less clear to me why there aren’t many new wildly successful hobbyist projects. Maybe it’s just hard to have a really good idea for a product, and AI can’t help with that. Or maybe it takes years for a really successful project to develop, and we need to be patient for the current crop of thousand-user tools to grow into hundred-thousand-user tools.

  1. As you might expect, this research was all done with the help of AI. It wasn’t purely vibed — I gave a lot of feedback about where and how to look — but I would definitely not have scraped or analyzed this much data on my own. If you want to see the actual research data (or more likely point an agent at it), I’ve pushed it here.

    ↩

  2. Sometimes scaling to take into account platform growth. For instance, between the two windows I measured, Obsidian relaxed their requirement that all new plugins be reviewed by an admin, which predictably caused an explosion of plugins on the marketplace.
